subject: ela
intro: Words that mean almost the same thing are called synonyms. But synonyms are not always interchangeable — some have stronger or more intense meanings than others. For example, warm, hot, and boiling all describe high temperature, but boiling is the strongest! In this lesson you will practice two skills: (1) sorting words into categories and identifying which word does not belong; and (2) understanding shades of meaning — ranking related words from weakest to strongest.

items.prompt: Sort these words into two categories — ANIMALS and FOODS: eagle, pizza, salmon, apple, bear, mango. Which category does each word belong to?

steps: Step 1 — Read each word and picture what it is.
Step 2 — eagle: a large bird — ANIMAL. Pizza: something you eat — FOOD. Salmon: a fish — ANIMAL. Apple: a fruit you eat — FOOD. Bear: a mammal — ANIMAL. Mango: a tropical fruit — FOOD.
Step 3 — ANIMALS: eagle, salmon, bear. FOODS: pizza, apple, mango.
solution.answer: Animals: eagle, salmon, bear. Foods: pizza, apple, mango.

items.prompt: Which word does NOT belong in this group: sad, upset, devastated, cheerful? Explain why.

steps: Step 1 — Think about what each word means. Sad = feeling unhappy. Upset = troubled and unhappy. Devastated = extremely sad and shocked. Cheerful = happy and bright.
Step 2 — Three words (sad, upset, devastated) all describe feeling unhappy. Cheerful describes the opposite — feeling happy.
Step 3 — Cheerful does NOT belong because all the other words describe sadness.
solution.answer: Cheerful does not belong. Sad, upset, and devastated all describe feelings of unhappiness, but cheerful means happy.

items.prompt: Arrange these words from least intense to most intense: hot, warm, boiling.

steps: Step 1 — Think about each temperature. Warm = pleasantly heated, like a sunny day. Hot = high temperature, like an oven. Boiling = extremely hot, like water that is bubbling.
Step 2 — Order from least to most: warm (mildly hot) → hot (very hot) → boiling (extremely hot).
Step 3 — Final order: warm, hot, boiling.
solution.answer: Least to most intense: warm, hot, boiling.

items.prompt: Here are three verbs: toss, throw, hurl. Arrange them from least to most forceful. Use each in a sentence to show the difference.

steps: Step 1 — Think about how much force each word suggests. Toss = a light, easy throw. Throw = a normal, moderate effort. Hurl = throwing with great force.
Step 2 — Order: toss (least force) → throw (medium force) → hurl (most force).
Step 3 — Sentences: 'She tossed the paper gently into the recycling bin.' 'He threw the ball across the yard.' 'The pitcher hurled the baseball with all his strength.'
solution.answer: Least to most forceful: toss, throw, hurl.

items.prompt: Which word best completes this sentence to describe an extreme feeling? 'After losing all her artwork in the flood, Maria was ___.' Choices: sad, upset, devastated.

steps: Step 1 — Consider the situation: Maria lost ALL her artwork in a flood. This is a very serious loss.
Step 2 — Sad = mildly unhappy; upset = troubled; devastated = deeply shocked and crushed by loss.
Step 3 — The situation is extreme, so the word should be the most intense. Devastated fits best.
Step 4 — Check: 'After losing all her artwork in the flood, Maria was devastated.' Yes — this conveys the deep sadness of a major loss.
solution.answer: Devastated best fits because losing all her artwork is a very serious and painful event.

items.prompt: Which word does NOT belong in this group: whisper, shout, murmur, mumble? Explain your reasoning.
items.hint: Think about how loud each action is. Which one is much louder than the others?

steps: Whisper = very quiet speaking. Murmur = soft, low sound. Mumble = speaking softly and unclearly. Shout = speaking very loudly.
Shout does NOT belong — it is the only loud word. The others all describe quiet speech.
solution.answer: Shout does not belong. Whisper, murmur, and mumble all describe quiet or soft speaking, but shout means speaking very loudly.

items.prompt: Arrange these adjectives from least to most intense: thin, slender, scrawny.
items.hint: Which word sounds the most polite? Which one makes you picture someone who looks too skinny?

steps: Slender = pleasantly thin and graceful. Thin = not heavy, average thinness. Scrawny = very thin in an unhealthy way.
Order: slender (positive, graceful) → thin (neutral) → scrawny (very thin, almost too thin).
Actually the typical intensity scale: thin (neutral) → slender (positively thin) → scrawny (negatively very thin). The intensity of 'thinness' goes: thin → slender → scrawny.
solution.answer: Least to most extreme thinness: thin, slender, scrawny.

items.prompt: Sort these words into two groups — THINGS YOU WEAR and THINGS YOU EAT: jacket, broccoli, boots, spaghetti, hat, blueberry.
items.hint: Picture each item. Can you put it on your body or put it in your mouth?

steps: Jacket = clothing — WEAR. Broccoli = vegetable — EAT. Boots = footwear — WEAR. Spaghetti = pasta — EAT. Hat = headwear — WEAR. Blueberry = fruit — EAT.
solution.answer: Things you wear: jacket, boots, hat. Things you eat: broccoli, spaghetti, blueberry.

items.prompt: Choose the most precise word to complete the sentence: 'The volcano erupted and shot _____ rocks into the sky.' Choices: warm, hot, scorching.
items.hint: How hot would rocks be coming from a volcano? Think about which word describes the most extreme heat.

steps: Rocks from a volcano are extremely hot — they are molten or just solidified from lava.
Warm = mildly heated (not nearly hot enough). Hot = quite hot. Scorching = intensely, painfully hot.
Scorching is the most precise and intense choice for rocks from a volcano.
solution.answer: Scorching. Volcano rocks are extremely hot, so scorching (the most intense word) is the most precise choice.

items.prompt: Explain the difference in meaning between these two sentences: (A) 'The puppy trotted across the yard.' (B) 'The puppy sprinted across the yard.' Which word signals more speed, trotted or sprinted? How do you know?
items.hint: Think about how fast each movement is. A trot is a light jog; a sprint is as fast as you can go.

steps: Trotted = moved at a light, easy jog — not very fast.
Sprinted = ran as fast as possible.
Sprinted signals much more speed than trotted.
You can tell because sprint describes maximum effort and speed, while trot describes a gentle pace.
solution.answer: Sprinted signals more speed. Trotted means moving at a light jog, while sprinted means running at full speed.
